context_notes: WHAT THE DOCUMENT IS. `docs/plans/2026-09-13-v0b-transport-plan.md` is a ~2,222-line implementation plan called 'Plan B' — the second of three plans for v0 of Notation Hero, a local-file drum-notation player. v0 opens a music file from disk, draws drum notation, and plays it. Plan A (already written) builds the AlphaTab playback engine, the `/play` screen and the test lane. Plan B (this document) builds the TRANSPORT: a seek bar that scrubs, a tempo control in the header, Loop / Metronome / Count-In toggles, and a progress bar for the soundfont download. Plan C builds the settings popovers. Nothing in Plan B has been implemented yet — reviewing it means reviewing INSTRUCTIONS and the code snippets those instructions tell an implementer to type, not shipped code.

HOW THE PLAN IS STRUCTURED. A `Global Constraints` section (rules every task inherits, including a list of verified facts about the `@coderline/alphatab` 1.8.4 library), a `File Structure` table, then nine numbered Tasks. Tasks 1-5 create five new presentation-only React components in the design-system package `client/` (`Slider`, `Progress`, `Scrubber`, `TransportToggle`, `TempoControl`), each built on a `@base-ui/react` primitive. Tasks 6-8 wire those components into the Next.js app package `web/`. Task 9 extends the accessibility gate and opens the pull request. Each Task is a numbered list of Steps with `- [ ]` checkboxes; most follow test-first order (write the failing test, run it, write the code, run it again, generate visual-regression baselines, commit).

SEVERITY SCALE USED HERE. P1 = the plan as written produces a broken or failing result if an implementer follows it literally — a test that cannot pass, a shipped bug, a false claim in the pull request. P2 = the plan works but leaves a real gap — a missing specification, an accessibility hole, a performance problem, or an unrecorded decision.

REVIEW HISTORY. Lap 1 ran three parallel review sweeps plus an adversarial audit and already landed 6 commits against this plan (a90390bf, 4b1dae50, 201956d8, 240ab626, 7630e19f, aa254817). A further 5 findings raised during THIS lap (lap 2) were already resolved mid-review by commit aa254817 ('fix(plans): correct the errors my own re-triage introduced') — those 5 are listed under `resolved_mid_review` below and are deliberately NOT in the `findings` list, so do not walk them.

When the quotes were verified against the installed `@coderline/alphatab` 1.8.4 source, the facts the plan states turned out to be CORRECT and the finding's basis turned out to be wrong. The finding is kept in the list so the reader can see it and drop it deliberately, with the counter-evidence recorded in its `evidence` field. Recommended disposition: Drop.

GLOSSARY of names that appear throughout. `AlphaTab` = the third-party JavaScript music-notation and playback library the player is built on; `api` = an `AlphaTabApi` instance, the object that renders notation and drives audio. `Base UI` (`@base-ui/react`) = the unstyled React component library every new control is built on. `soundfont` = the ~302 KB file of audio samples AlphaTab downloads before it can make sound. `VR` = visual-regression tests (Playwright pixel screenshots of Storybook stories, baselines committed as Linux PNGs). `axe` / `a11y` = automated accessibility auditing; both VR and axe block merge in CI. `e2e` = Playwright end-to-end tests against the built app. `playbackSpeed` = an AlphaTab property, a multiplier where 1 is the score's written tempo. `HUMAN GATE` = a step the plan marks as impossible for a machine (needs human ears or a human browser console); an agent must stop and hand back rather than self-certify it.

findings.section: Task 2 (`Progress`) — creating a brand-new `Progress` bar component in the design-system package `client/`, wrapping the `@base-ui/react/progress` primitive. This is the bar that shows how much of the soundfont (AlphaTab's ~302 KB audio-sample file) has downloaded. The finding spans three places inside Task 2: the explanatory callout before Step 1 (lines 484-489), the unit tests the plan tells the implementer to write in Step 1 (lines 517-533), and the component itself in Step 3 (lines 567-582).
findings.title: Two of `Progress`'s own tests fail on first run, and the shipped bar announces an out-of-range percentage
findings.whats_wrong: The plan states three times that the Base UI `Progress` primitive clamps its value into [min, max]. It does not. `ProgressRoot` passes the value straight through to the DOM as `'aria-valuenow': value ?? undefined`, with no clamp anywhere in the primitive. The wrapper multiplies the incoming fraction by 100 and hands it over unmodified, so the two tests the plan writes in Step 1 — one feeding `value={1.8}` and expecting `aria-valuenow="100"`, one feeding `value={-0.5}` and expecting `aria-valuenow="0"` — will instead see `"180"` and `"-50"` and fail. Step 4 says 'Expected: PASS — 4 tests', so an implementer following the plan hits two red tests with no instruction on what to do, and the most likely repair (loosening the tests) ships a progress bar that tells a screen reader the download is 180 percent complete. The over-unity case is not hypothetical: the plan's own comment explains that `total` is the ENCODED byte length while `loaded` counts DECODED bytes when the CDN compresses the response, so the ratio genuinely exceeds 1.
findings.proposed_fix: Clamp the fraction inside the wrapper — `Math.min(100, Math.max(0, value * 100))` — before handing it to `ProgressPrimitive.Root`, and correct all three comments that credit the primitive with clamping (the pre-Step-1 callout, the test comment, and the component doc comment). Leave both `test(...)` blocks untouched: the assertions are right, only the explanation of who does the clamping was wrong.
findings.why_it_works: The two tests were written to encode the correct product behaviour — a progress bar must never announce more than 100 percent or less than 0. Moving the clamp from an imagined library guarantee into one explicit expression in the wrapper makes both tests pass on first run AND makes the behaviour true at runtime, which loosening the tests would not. The clamp is three tokens; it also fixes the visual indicator, whose width comes from the same unclamped value (an 180% width would overflow the track).
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: An implementer runs Step 4, gets 2 failures against a step that says 'Expected: PASS — 4 tests', and has no instruction covering it. The cheapest repair is to change the tests to expect `'180'` and `'-50'`, which ships a bar that reads 'one hundred and eighty percent' to a screen-reader user and paints an indicator wider than its own track, whenever the CDN serves the soundfont compressed.
findings.evidence:
Verified against the installed `@base-ui/react` 1.6.0 in this worktree (node_modules/.pnpm/@base-ui+react@1.6.0_.../node_modules/@base-ui/react/):
- `progress/root/ProgressRoot.js` builds its DOM props as `'aria-valuenow': value ?? undefined` — no clamp, no `Math.min`/`Math.max`.

findings.section: Task 6 Step 1 (`Write the failing tests`) — Task 6 wires the transport row (Loop, Metronome, Count-In and the seek bar) into the app's `PlayerShell` and connects each control to the AlphaTab engine. Its Step 1 adds two Playwright end-to-end tests to `web/e2e/player.e2e.ts`; the second, `'the scrubber seeks and the position follows'`, is the automated half of acceptance criterion 6 ('the scrubber seeks and the cursor follows'). It focuses the seek slider, presses ArrowRight five times (five one-second steps), then polls the engine to confirm the playhead really moved.
findings.title: The seek test cannot fail on a seek the engine refuses
findings.whats_wrong: The test deliberately avoids reading the app's own state — the comment explains that the app writes `setPositionMs(ms)` optimistically, so a mirrored DOM attribute would report the requested value even on a broken seek. It then reads `api.timePosition` instead, believing that to be the engine's own clock. In a browser with the audio worker enabled it is not. `api.timePosition` is served by `AlphaSynthWebWorkerApi`, whose setter stores the requested value into a local `_currentPosition` object BEFORE posting `alphaSynth.setTimePosition` to the worker, and whose getter returns that stored value. So the read echoes whatever was written — exactly the failure mode the comment set out to avoid, just moved one layer down. The same setter copies `currentTick` through untouched, so the TICK position is the value that only moves once a real position update comes back from the worker.
findings.proposed_fix: Read `api.tickPosition` instead of `api.timePosition` through the same debug handle, rename the helper to `engineTickPosition`, assert `toBeGreaterThan(0)` (a tick count is not comparable to a millisecond threshold — it depends on the score's tempo and MIDI division), and rewrite the comment to say which of the two values the worker actually confirms and why.
findings.why_it_works: It restores the falsifiability the test was designed for. The tick is the one field the worker-backed setter does not fabricate locally: `set timePosition` builds a new `PositionChangedEventArgs(value, …, this._currentPosition.currentTick, …)` — new time, carried-over tick. If the worker never processes the seek, the tick stays at 0 and the poll times out, which is what a broken seek should do. The score is paused throughout the test (it never presses play), so nothing else can move the tick.
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: Acceptance criterion 6 ships with a test that passes on a completely broken seek — the assertion reads back the number the test itself caused to be written. Because the by-eye cursor check is a HUMAN GATE that an agent must hand back rather than perform, a regression in seeking would reach master with a green CI lane and an unticked human box, i.e. nobody checking either way.

findings.section: Task 8 Step 1 (`Write the failing test`) — Task 8 builds the soundfont progress bar: while AlphaTab downloads its ~302 KB file of audio samples, a determinate bar shows how far along it is. Step 1 adds a Playwright end-to-end test asserting the bar appears during the download and is gone afterwards. Because the download is normally sub-second, the test has to slow it down artificially to make the bar observable at all — and Task 8 Step 4 renders the bar only after progress has been running ~300 ms (a deliberate anti-strobe delay).
findings.title: The progress-bar test times out, because the stall it uses cannot widen the window it needs
findings.whats_wrong: The test stalls the soundfont by intercepting its route and awaiting a 4-second `setTimeout` before calling `route.continue()`. That delays when the request STARTS; it does nothing to the transfer once it starts. AlphaTab's progress events (`soundFontLoad`, which carries `{ loaded, total }`) only begin firing once bytes are arriving, so the whole progress window is still the same sub-second transfer — just shifted four seconds later. Task 8 Step 4's rendering rule requires progress to have been running for 300 ms before the bar mounts at all, so on a fast local transfer the bar may never render, and `await expect(bar).toBeVisible({ timeout: 30_000 })` times out. The test is red for a reason unrelated to the feature.
findings.proposed_fix: Replace the request-delay stall with browser-level network throttling applied before the page loads: open a Chrome DevTools Protocol session on the page (`page.context().newCDPSession(page)`), enable the Network domain, and call `Network.emulateNetworkConditions` with a download throughput around 150 KB/s. Keep the rest of the test unchanged.
findings.why_it_works: Throttling changes the transfer RATE rather than the start time, so the ~302 KB soundfont genuinely takes around two seconds to arrive. AlphaTab emits `soundFontLoad` progress events across that whole window, the 300 ms appear-delay elapses with progress still running, the bar mounts and is observable, and it still clears well inside the existing 60-second `transport-play` timeout. It also exercises the feature the way a real slow connection would — which is the only condition under which this bar is ever meant to appear.
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: Step 5 says 'Expected: PASS' but the lane goes red on a 30-second timeout with no visible cause, and the obvious repairs are both wrong: raising the timeout does not create a progress window, and deleting the 300 ms delay re-introduces the strobe the delay exists to prevent. The likely outcome is that the only automated coverage of the progress bar gets skipped or deleted.
findings.evidence: Basis from the review: delaying the start of a request does not stretch its transfer; the sub-second transfer stays under the 300 ms appear-delay. This is consistent with the plan's own two statements: Task 8's preamble (line 1924) sizes the soundfont at '302 KB gzip of the ~1.6 MB first-load payload', and Task 8 Step 4 (lines 2018-2022) states 'On a normal connection this download is a sub-second window — the e2e case below has to stall the request by four seconds just to make the bar observable — so rendering it the instant progress starts produces a strobe… Show it only once the download has been running ~300 ms'. findings.section: Task 6 Step 5 (`Wire the shell to the api`) — the step that adds playback state to `web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx` and subscribes to AlphaTab's `playerPositionChanged` event. That event fires as audio plays and carries the current playhead time, the song length and the live tempo. The handler shown in the plan writes all three into React state, which means every one of those events re-renders the whole player shell and everything under it (the header, the tempo pill, the transport row, the scrubber).
findings.title: The transport re-renders hundreds of times a second during playback
findings.whats_wrong: `playerPositionChanged` is not a tidy once-per-frame event. In the browser's audio-worklet path, the worklet posts a `samplesPlayed` message on every audio render quantum — 128 audio frames — and each of those drives one `positionChanged` trigger. At a 44.1 kHz sample rate that is about 345 events per second. The handler as written calls `setPositionMs`, `setDurationMs` and `setScoreTempo` on every one of them, so React commits roughly 345 times a second while the score plays, against a subtree that includes the notation surface's siblings. A display that updates in whole seconds (the scrubber's `mm:ss` clock) and a BPM readout are being driven about six times faster than the screen can even show.
findings.proposed_fix: Coalesce the handler to at most one React commit per animation frame: keep the latest event arguments in a ref, schedule a single `requestAnimationFrame` if none is pending, and do the three `set*` calls inside that frame. Cancel any pending frame on unmount. Leave both existing guards running on every event, unthrottled.
findings.why_it_works: It decouples the audio event rate (~345/s, fixed by the Web Audio 128-frame quantum) from the render rate (~60/s, the fastest the display can show anything), collapsing about six events into one commit with no loss of information — the ref always holds the newest value, so the frame paints the current position, not a stale one. Keeping the guards outside the throttle preserves their meaning: guard 1 rejects the subscribe-time stub and guard 2 drops the post-seek stale burst; both are correctness filters that must see every event, and throttling them would let a stale event through as 'the latest'.
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: Playback drives roughly 345 React commits per second over the header, the tempo pill and the whole transport row. On a low-powered laptop that competes for main-thread time with AlphaTab's own cursor animation and notation scrolling, and audio glitching is the visible symptom — on the one screen whose entire purpose is smooth playback. It is also the kind of problem that is invisible in CI and only shows up on a real machine with a real score.

Verified against the installed `@coderline/alphatab` 1.8.4 (dist/alphaTab.core.mjs):
- `AlphaSynthWebWorkletProcessor.process(...)` (inside `class AlphaSynthWebWorklet`, line 41490) ends every invocation with `this.port.postMessage({ cmd: "alphaSynth.output.samplesPlayed", samples: samplesFromBuffer / SynthConstants.AudioChannels });`. `process` is called once per Web Audio render quantum = 128 frames, so 44100 / 128 ≈ 344.5 messages per second.
- `AlphaSynthAudioWorkletOutput._handleMessage` routes `alphaSynth.output.samplesPlayed` to `this.onSamplesPlayed(data.samples)`.
- `AlphaSynthBase._onSamplesPlayed(sampleCount)` calls `this.updateTimePosition(this._timePosition + playedMillis, false)`.
- `AlphaSynthBase.updateTimePosition` ends with `if (this.sequencer.isPlayingMain) { this._currentPosition = args; this.positionChanged.trigger(args); }`.
So one position event per audio quantum, one handler run per event, three `set*` calls per run.

findings.section: Task 9 Step 3 (`🧑 HUMAN GATE — Measure every new control's hit area`) — Task 9 is the final task: it extends the accessibility (axe) gate and opens the PR. Step 3 asks the maintainer to start the dev server, open the browser console on a loaded `/play`, and paste a snippet that measures every control and lists any smaller than 44 CSS pixels. The 44 px rule is one of the plan's Global Constraints (line 80). Plan A already ships an automated version of this check — an `expectHitAreas(page, label)` helper in `web/e2e/a11y.e2e.ts`.
findings.title: The 44 px hit-area rule has no automated guard, and the existing automated one misses the new slider rails
findings.whats_wrong: Step 3 is marked as a HUMAN GATE, but nothing in it needs a human: the snippet is pure DOM measurement — `querySelectorAll`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `filter` — which Playwright's `page.evaluate` runs unattended. Marking it human-only spends one of the plan's four hand-back moments on something a machine does better, and produces a one-time check that cannot stop a later control shrinking. Worse, Plan A's automated helper already exists but its selector is `'button, a[href], label[for], [role="button"]'` — it does not match the slider rail this plan adds, whose 44 px pointer target lives on the slider's `Control` element (`h-11`), not on any button. Plan B's own manual snippet does include that selector, so the plan proves the gap exists and then leaves the automated gate blind to it.

findings.section: Global Constraints — specifically the sub-list at lines 96-131 headed '`@coderline/alphatab` 1.8.4 facts this plan relies on — all verified against the installed `dist/alphaTab.d.ts` and, where marked **observed**, against a headless run of the real synth'. The plan builds two guards on that behaviour (Task 6 Step 5, lines 1653-1682). NOTE: this finding is DISPUTED — see `evidence`.
findings.title: DISPUTED — the review claims two 'observed' engine facts are wrong for the browser build; verification says the plan is right
findings.whats_wrong:
The review's claim: the two replay-related facts were observed on a headless no-worker synth run, and do not hold in a browser, which runs the worker-backed facade whose event emitters are constructed bare — with no replay provider. On that reading, guard 1 (which drops the subscribe-time `120 BPM` stub) would be defending against something that never happens in the browser, and the Task 6 comment claiming `midiLoaded` 'also replays for late subscribers' would be false. The proposed change was: note that the replay providers exist only on the direct no-worker path, downgrade guard 1 to defence-in-depth, and delete the 'also replays for late subscribers' sentence.

On verification this claim does not hold. The review looked at `AlphaSynthWebWorkerApi` (whose emitters are indeed bare) but missed `AlphaSynthWrapper`, which sits between that class and the public API and DOES construct replay providers on every path. Both plan statements are correct as written; nothing is wrong.

findings.evidence:
Verified against the installed `@coderline/alphatab` 1.8.4 (dist/alphaTab.core.mjs). The review's premise is half true and its conclusion is wrong:
- TRUE: `class AlphaSynthWebWorkerApi` (line 33477) declares its emitters bare — `positionChanged = new EventEmitterOfT();`, `midiLoaded = new EventEmitterOfT();` — with no `fireOnRegister` provider.
- MISSED: `api.playerPositionChanged` does not return that object. `AlphaTabApiBase.get playerPositionChanged() { return this._player.positionChanged; }`, and `this._player` is an `AlphaSynthWrapper` (line 44976). Its constructor reads:
    `this.positionChanged = new EventEmitterOfT(() => { return this.currentPosition; });`
    `this.midiLoaded = new EventEmitterOfT(() => { return this._instance?.loadedMidiInfo ?? null; });`
  — replay providers, present on every path.
- `AlphaSynthWrapper.get currentPosition()` returns `this._instance ? this._shiftPositionChangedEventArgsToApi(this._instance.currentPosition) : new PositionChangedEventArgs(0, 0, 0, 0, false, 120, 120)` — and `AlphaSynthWebWorkerApi._currentPosition` is itself initialised to `new PositionChangedEventArgs(0, 0, 0, 0, false, 120, 120)`. findings.section: Task 5 (`TempoControl` — the header pill) — the new component showing the current tempo in beats per minute with `-` and `+` steppers, built on Base UI's `NumberField`. Alongside the BPM number it shows a percentage (how fast playback is relative to the score's written tempo), governed by a four-part visibility rule in the plan at lines 1063-1077: shown on focus, shown on hover, hidden on blur or 3 seconds after a change, and never shown at exactly 100 %. The finding concerns a prop called `showPercent` that exists only to force that percentage visible.
findings.title: A shipped public prop exists only to drive stories and screenshots
findings.whats_wrong: `showPercent` is declared in the component's public props, documented in the Interfaces line, and read at runtime in the expression `data-linger={showPercent ?? lingering}`. Its own doc comment says what it is for: 'For stories and VR only; leave undefined in the app.' That is a test affordance living in production API surface — every consumer of the design system sees a prop they must know not to use, and nothing enforces that. The repo has a standing rule against exactly this ('test-only instrumentation never ships; test the real thing'). It is also unnecessary: Task 5 Step 5 already explains that two of the three visibility triggers are pure CSS, so the existing `hover` and `focus` visual-regression states capture the visible percentage and `resting` captures its absence — the paragraph at lines 1388-1391 offers `showPercent` only as an optional extra snapshot nobody needs.
findings.proposed_fix: Remove `showPercent` from `TempoControlProps`, from the component's destructured parameters, from the `data-linger` expression (leaving `data-linger={lingering}`), and from the Interfaces signature at line 1049. Rewrite the optional-snapshot paragraph to say plainly that the linger needs no snapshot because it paints the same state `hover` and `focus` already capture.
findings.why_it_works: The prop's only stated purpose is already covered: the linger produces the identical visual state that the `hover` and `focus` snapshots capture, differing only in what triggered it — and a pixel screenshot cannot see a trigger. Deleting it removes a public prop that every future consumer would have to be told not to use, and honours the repo's standing rule against shipping test-only instrumentation. It costs nothing: no test in Task 5 Step 1 references `showPercent`.
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: A design-system component ships with a prop whose documentation is an instruction not to use it. Nothing stops an app developer setting `showPercent` to pin the percentage permanently visible, which silently defeats the whole four-part visibility rule (including rule 4, 'never shown at 100 %'), and the component's own tests would not catch it.
findings.evidence: The prop's doc comment at line 1220 states its purpose outright: '/** Force the percentage visible. For stories and VR only; leave undefined in the app. */'. Task 5 Step 5's own paragraph (lines 1375-1378, and 1388-1391) argues the CSS triggers make a dedicated story unnecessary: 'With the rule above, two of the three triggers are CSS, so the existing states cover them'. None of the eleven tests in Task 5 Step 1 (lines 1090-1190) passes `showPercent`. Repo memory rule, 'No test code in prod': test-only instrumentation never ships; test the real thing.

findings.section: Task 5 (`TempoControl`, the header BPM pill) and Task 6 Step 5 (the `PlayerShell` wiring that keeps `scoreTempo` live). Background: the pill displays BPM but OWNS a speed multiplier — the displayed number is `scoreTempo × speed`, and when the user edits the number the component converts back with `nextBpm / scoreTempo`. Meanwhile Task 6 Step 5 updates `scoreTempo` continuously from AlphaTab's position events, because a score's tempo can change part-way through (a tempo automation) and the header should show the tempo where the playhead currently is.
findings.title: The tempo a drummer just typed moves on its own as the playhead crosses a tempo change
findings.whats_wrong: `handleBpm` converts the typed or stepped BPM into a speed by dividing by whatever `scoreTempo` holds at that instant. But `scoreTempo` is a live value being rewritten roughly 345 times a second by the position handler. On a score with a tempo automation (say 90 → 120 BPM at bar 9), a user who types `100` while the playhead is still in the 90 section gets `speed = 100/90 ≈ 1.111`; seconds later the playhead crosses into the 120 section, `scoreTempo` becomes 120, and the same unchanged speed now displays as `Math.round(120 × 1.111) = 133`. The number the user set has moved by itself. A hold-to-repeat press makes it worse: the buttons tick every 60 ms, so a single held press can straddle an automation boundary and each tick divides by a different denominator. Neither the component nor the plan says anywhere that the readout intentionally tracks the playhead, so the behaviour reads as a bug even to someone who understands the model.
findings.proposed_fix: Snapshot the score tempo when an edit or stepper interaction begins (`onPointerDown` / `onFocus`), convert against that snapshot inside `handleBpm`, and clear it when the interaction ends (`onPointerUp` / `onBlur`). Add a unit test proving a mid-edit `scoreTempo` change does not move the result, and state explicitly in the component's doc comment that the readout is meant to track the playhead while the conversion is not.
findings.why_it_works: It separates two behaviours that are currently tangled into one variable. The DISPLAY should follow the playhead — that is the whole reason Task 6 keeps `scoreTempo` live, and the plan is right about it. The CONVERSION should not: a single user gesture must resolve against a single denominator, or the value the user set is not the value they get. Pinning only the conversion, for only the duration of one interaction, fixes the second without touching the first. Writing the intent into the doc comment is the other half of the fix — without it the moving readout still looks like a defect to the next reader.
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: On any score with a tempo change — common in real drum charts — the header number drifts away from what the user just set, and the drift is silent and unexplained. Because the bundled sample score used by the by-ear human gate is unlikely to carry an automation, neither the gate nor CI will surface it; it appears only when a user opens their own file, which is the entire point of a local-file player.
findings.evidence: Line 1258 is the conversion: `const next = Math.min(maxSpeed, Math.max(minSpeed, nextBpm / scoreTempo));` — `scoreTempo` is a prop, not a captured value. Line 1678 (Task 6 Step 5) rewrites it on every position event: `setScoreTempo(args.originalTempo); // live; score.tempo is the INITIAL tempo only`. The plan itself documents both that automations exist and that `originalTempo` follows them, at Global Constraints lines 115-119: '**`score.tempo` is the INITIAL tempo only.** … on a score whose tempo changes it reports the opening value for the whole piece (**observed**: a 90 → 120 → 60 score reported 90 throughout). Use `args.originalTempo`, which is recomputed from the MIDI tempo table on every position update and tracks automations at bar and sub-bar granularity (**observed** flipping exactly at the automation ticks).' The 60 ms hold-repeat tick is stated at lines 1055-1056: 'hold-to-repeat on the buttons (`START_AUTO_CHANGE_DELAY = 400` then a tick every `CHANGE_VALUE_TICK_DELAY = 60`)'.

findings.section: Task 1 (`Slider` — the single-value primitive, the new design-system component wrapping Base UI's `Slider`) and Task 3 (`Scrubber` — current time, seek bar, total time, which composes `Slider`), with the consequence landing in Task 6 Step 5 (the `seek` callback in `PlayerShell` that writes `api.timePosition`). This one is filed as a DECISION rather than a proposed fix because it changes a public component's API and how continuous dragging feels, which is a product call, not a defect repair.
findings.title: DECISION — one drag across the seek bar issues hundreds of engine seeks
findings.whats_wrong: `Slider` wires Base UI's continuous `onValueChange` straight to its own `onChange`. `Scrubber` turns every one of those into `onSeek(seconds * 1000)`, and `PlayerShell`'s `seek` callback turns every one of THOSE into `api.timePosition = ms`. So a single drag across the bar — which emits a value on every pointer move — issues one engine seek per pointer event. Each seek is not cheap: in the worker-backed browser path it posts an `alphaSynth.setTimePosition` message, and the direct synth path behind it runs `sequencer.mainSeek(value)` plus, while playing, `output.resetSamples()` — a full audio buffer flush. Dragging therefore floods the worker with seek messages and repeatedly dumps the audio buffer. It also interacts badly with the post-seek stale-event guard the plan already carries (Task 6 Step 5, guard 2): each new seek overwrites `pendingSeek.current`, so the guard is re-armed on every pointer move and the 250 ms bound keeps restarting.
findings.proposed_fix: The review recommends OPTION A: add an optional `onCommit` callback to `Slider`, mapped to Base UI's `onValueCommitted` event, and have `Scrubber` seek from that while `onChange` keeps the thumb and the elapsed clock tracking the pointer.
findings.why_it_works: Base UI already separates the two events, so nothing has to be hand-built: `onValueChange` fires continuously, `onValueCommitted` fires once at the end of the interaction (pointer release, or a settled keystroke). Mapping each to its natural job puts the cheap work on the cheap event and the expensive work on the rare one — one drag becomes one seek. Keyboard seeking (the path the e2e test uses, five ArrowRight presses) still works, because `onValueCommitted` fires for keyboard changes too. Putting the seam in `Slider` rather than in `PlayerShell` also means Plan C's settings rows and per-track volume sliders inherit it instead of each re-solving the same problem.
findings.consequence_if_unchanged: Dragging the seek bar floods the audio worker with seek messages and flushes the sample buffer on each one, at exactly the moment the user is interacting most intensely. The likely symptom is audible stutter or a visibly laggy thumb while scrubbing. It will not show up in CI — the e2e test seeks with the keyboard, which emits one value per keypress and never exercises a drag — and the by-eye human gate (Task 6 Step 7) asks the maintainer to 'drag the scrubber to the middle', which on a fast development machine may well feel fine.
